title: Reporting
text:
Annual Reporting
In Baton Rouge, the open data policy requires annual reporting by the Director of Information Services (Baton Rouge and Parish of East Baton Rouge 2017).

“The report shall include an assessment of progress toward achievement of the goals of the City-Parish’s Open Data BR program (under which all City-Parish open data related activities occur), an assessment of how the City-Parish’s work has furthered or will further the City-Parish’s programmatic priorities, and a description and publication timeline for datasets envisioned to be published by the City-Parish in the following year.”

Since 2018, they have published annual reports (Baton Rouge and Parish of East Baton Rouge, n.d.-a), which are often published directly on their open data platform, such as the most recent 2025 Open Data Policy Report (Baton Rouge and Parish of East Baton Rouge 2025).

title: Reporting
text:
Blogs
Other ways of sharing information about initiatives powered by open data include blog posts. In San Francisco, the first Chief Data Officer explained the strategic vision of the program (Bonaguro 2014) , initiated by the updated open data policy (City and County of San Francisco 2013), and the progress made to institutionalize data practices provided by the current Chief Data Officer (Team 2026).
Civic technology and advocacy organizations in Austin have published advocacy agendas (Open Austin 2016) and contributions through new data, analysis, and advocacy (Carey 2020, 2016; Rosenthal 2013; Open Austin, n.d.).

title: Reporting
text:
Dashboards
Asset inventories available on data portals provide views of all assets, like the Austin Open Data Asset Inventory Dashboard (City of Austin, n.d.). Programs may also add other information to asset inventories like the department assigned value of a dataset, publishing status (some data may only be available internally), update frequency, and monthly views like the San Francisco Dataset Inventory Explorer (City and County of San Francisco, n.d.).
Views of applications that span multiple data platforms can be shown on custom dashboards such as the Transparency Performance Metrics dashboard (Baton Rouge and Parish of East Baton Rouge, n.d.-b) that includes lifetime views of map applications, web tools, department priority dashboards, and citizen data academy video tutorials.

title: Engagement Measures
text:
Engagement with open data can be detected by public interactions with programs and the activity of community organizations, local news organizations, and other intermediaries. The presence of articles demonstrates accessibility of department data for local reporting and public interest.
Requests made by the public are valuable opportunities to gather feedback and build trust by responding to matters that are meaningful and personally important to members of the public (Guy 2021).
The potential for journalists and researchers to act as intermediaries of open data by synthesizing open data into useful information (Shaharudin et al. 2023), creating feedback loops to government (Wilson and Chakraborty 2019), and hosting datathon events(Kopf 2022).

title: Engagement Measures
text:
Interaction Measures
Support and Customer Relationship Management platforms makes it possible to report on the types of requests made by the public and resolution information.

title: Engagement Measures
text:
Engagement Measures
Views of content, social media registration and reach, newsletter registration, and attendance events demonstrate interest and engagement with programs and community organizations.

title: Engagement Measures
text:
Activity Measures
Public activity may be detected as new articles and tools created externally that reference open data or contribute new data.
Measures include the publication, date, topic, department data owners, links to data, and contributions made by the publication staff of new data, visualizations, and tools created in support of the article.
In addition to counting the number of events and attendees, there are other measures that show the contributions made by the public. Examples of important hackathon measures include new ideas, viable design concepts, prototypes, participant social connections, new start-ups, and increased domain and technical knowledge gains for participants (Jaskiewicz et al. 2019).

title: Engagement Measures
text:
Data Collection
Articles may be tracked through manual monitoring of websites and blogs of local organizations as well as by setting up alerts, such as with Google Alerts. Articles may be tracked in citation tools, like Zotero, which provides rich organization features and export of data as CSV file. Articles can also be maintained manually in a spreadsheet.
Contributions by community organizations can be found on websites and by registering to mailing lists and attending events.
The civic engagement community organization, Open Austin, has served Austin since 2009. They successfully advocated for the creation of the open data portal (Dunbar 2009), served as members of the local Code for America chapter, and continue to be active in helping their community to have access to data to improve local conditions and policies. Read more about their projects and fellowships.
The civic technology community organization, SF Civic Tech, has served San Francisco since 2013, where they began as the local Code for America chapter ((Re-)introducing SF Civic Tech 2024). Read more about their projects and events.

title: Organizational Actions
text: Actions taken to support the use of open data indicate organizational commitment to transparency and share what data is collected and being used to provide public services and inform government response to community issues.

title: Organizational Actions
text:
Dataset and Data Product Measures
New datasets often represent the fulfillment of public requests (Mergel et al. 2018) or commitment of departments and programs to publish data that shows how their work serves the public (Johnson 2016). Government response to public health emergencies, severe weather events, and local issues can be measured in part by the new applications and websites created to provide information and connect people to needed services.
The Information Services team at Baton Rouge created a map application to inform and guide their response to a major flood event (Koma 2016). They also invited the public to contact their department directly to update them about property damage (Gallo 2016). The flood inundation map continues to rank as one of the top data products accessed by the public (Baton Rouge and Parish of East Baton Rouge, n.d.).
Senate bills passed by the state authorizing immigration checks by public safety departments led to the city council in Austin to pass a resolution directing the Police Department to end most arrests for citation-eligible offenses and to provide detailed data about discretionary arrests for leadership review (Wilson 2018; City of Austin 2018). The publishing of the Immigration Status Dataset and Guide (City of Austin and Austin Police Department, n.d.-b, n.d.-a) to the open data portal enabled both internal and external reviews of arrests and racial disparities (Sanders 2020; Gates et al. 2020; Cronk 2020).
By providing the context of new dataset and data products, organizations can demonstrate how open data supports the priorities of local government and the public.

title: Organizational Actions
text:
Support Measures
Content created to train users on how to use open data and data products demonstrate program commitment to the public. Dedicated communication channels for technical support or to ask data owners questions demonstrate accountability for the systems and data published on data portals.

title: Organizational Actions
text:
Event Measures
Open data day celebrations, datathons, and hackathons are ways that open data programs, departments, community organizations, researchers, local news organizations, and technology sponsors typically engage the public to participate in a day, weekend, or week of using government data to help understand and tackle important community issues. The number of events hosted and supported are measures that demonstrate program engagement with the public.

title: Organizational Actions
text:
Organization Change Measures
Additions to staffing or changes to groups to ensure there is adequate staff to publish new data, address increases in data work, and facilitate coordination show commitment to making data publicly available.
An example of an organization change in Baton Rouge made to improve analytics capacity is the integration of the GIS staff with the Information Services team to form a unified Division of Data, Analytics and Performance team and the creation of a dedicated outreach coordinator position (Baton Rouge and Parish of East Baton Rouge 2023).

title: Organizational Actions
text:
Data Collection
The number of new datasets and some data products may be found from the catalogs provided by data portals and filtered by creation date and asset type. Context may also be available for those assets if that information has been added to the description, category, data owner, and other metadata fields. New applications and websites that are created outside of a data portal will require manual collection but likely will be tracked by an internal system used for department and technical support teams.
Events may be manually tracked by departments spreadsheets or available through event registration software.
New and updated systems that provide support and facilitate communication may be tracked through internal project portfolio systems.

title: Organizational Actions
text:
Reporting
Reporting organizational actions should include narrative that describes the context and motivations for the actions. Ongoing reporting may show lifetime values of actions and results. Annual reporting provides a snapshot for the program, enabling tracking of progress over time.
A consistent feature of the Baton Rouge annual open data policy report is the “By the Numbers” section that shows both the number of datasets, data products, events, and engagements, as well as the resulting social media impressions and views of data assets and support videos (Baton Rouge and Parish of East Baton Rouge 2025).

title: About
text:
The toolkit identifies the types of measures that signal public use and engagement with open data and provides recommendations for regular reporting of actions and resulting activity.
The development of the open data actions and measures toolkit fulfills one part of a dissertation portfolio that focuses on measuring open data use and engagement to serve and empower the public.
Source code: https://github.com/aliciatb/open-data-action-toolkit

title: Data Portal Measures
text:
Web analytics provides raw data on all assets on a data portal. Analytics combined with metadata and dataset information provide a holistic view of how people are accessing open data that can be presented to data owners and the public.
Dataset characteristics like category, agency function, expected user group, information type, and related open government principle have been used to evaluate the public usefulness of a data catalog (Schwoerer 2022). The evaluation of metadata completion, communication mechanisms, and publishing frequency provides a way to track the commitment of a program to providing open data (Nahon et al. 2015).

title: Data Portal Measures
text:
Web Analytic Measures
Data portals typically provide the number of views of assets, downloads of datasets, and programmatic requests to the API (application programming interface) endpoints of assets.
Additional measures of quality may be inferred by the contents of data catalogs and capabilities of data portals.

title: Data Portal Measures
text:
Data Collection
Data portals displage the lifetime page views for data assets on individual overview pages, data catalog listings, and through APIs (application programming interface). Tyler Technologies and Esri provide documentation on their use (Tyler Technologies 2022), (Esri, n.d.).

Overview Pages
Dataset overview pages provide important details about the data and lifetime page views and downloads. An example of an overview page is the Issued Construction Permits on the Austin data portal.



Issued Building Permits


In the “About” section, the lifetime views and downloads are shown, which for this dataset consist of 5.38 million views and 82.3 thousand downloads.


Data Catalogs
Data catalogs enable user to search for relevant data and also sort results by assets with the most views. The Tyler Technology open data platform also includes the lifetime views of assets.
As organizations often maintain multiple data portals for geospatial and tabular data, it is important to check whether they have multiple sites and if data is federated to a single portal to facilitate public discovery of data.
Example data catalogs include:

Austin, Texas

Data catalog: https://data.austintexas.gov/browse
Maps and applications catalog: https://austin.maps.arcgis.com/home/gallery.html

Baton Rouge, Louisiana

Data catalog: https://data.brla.gov/browse
Maps and applications catalog: https://data-ebrgis.opendata.arcgis.com/search

San Francisco, California

Data catalog: https://data.sf.gov/browse
Maps and applications catalog: https://sfgov.maps.arcgis.com/home/gallery.html




APIs (Application programming interfaces)
The Tyler Technologies Discovery API (Socrata Discovery API, n.d.) provides analytic details for all data assets on a data portal that includes lifetime views and downloads, as well as views in the last week and month, providing insights on current public interest. Authentication is not required to access information about published data assets on domain. Tools like Excel and Power BI can easily connect to the API endpoint to make information available for analysis.
In the tylertech_discovery.xlsx spreadsheet and tylertech_catalog_analytics.pbix Power BI dashboard available for download, the following data catalogs were queried and combined to demonstrate how to retrieve and easily refresh web analytic and metadata information.

Below are the API endpoints with parameters to retrieve all published data assets by data portal domain.

Austin, Texas

Discovery catalog endpoint: http://api.us.socrata.com/api/catalog/v1?search_context=data.austintexas.gov&published=true&limit=5000

Baton Rouge, Louisiana

Discovery catalog endpoint: http://api.us.socrata.com/api/catalog/v1?search_context=data.brla.gov&published=true&limit=5000

San Francisco, California

Discovery catalog endpoint: http://api.us.socrata.com/api/catalog/v1?search_context=data.sf.gov&published=true&limit=5000

title: A Guide for Measuring Open Data Use
text:
The open data action toolkit provides guidance on how to measure organizational actions and public engagement with open data. The actions and measures shared in the toolkit were identified from literature review of existing research on open data use and measures, supplemented with findings from case studies of 3 local governments in the United States.
The examples provided in the toolkit are based on the data, data products, and reporting created by case study participants from the City of Austin, the City of Baton Rouge and Parish of East Baton Rouge, and the City and County of San Francisco open data programs. Community developed analysis, tools, and data products are also presented here demonstrating the important role of open data intermediaries to synthesize government data, create innovative tools for exploring data, and advocate on behalf of the public.

Organizational Action Measures
The toolkit first provides examples of the types of actions taken by organizations to support open data use, including:

The creation of data products (datasets, maps, applications, dashboards, visualizations, data stories, and initiative websites) in support of public information requests, department initiatives, leadership priorities, directives or resolutions, technology standards or policies, community issues, or emergency events
The provision of support and communication mechanisms
Hosting and participating in local events
Organization and staffing changes

Learn more about tracking organizational action measures.


Data Portal Measures
The toolkit then demonstrates how to measure direct use of data and other assets published on data portals from data portal anayltics. Measures include:

Views of datasets, maps, dashboards, visualizations, and data stories
Dataset downloads
Requests to API (application programming interface) endpoints by analysis tools and code
Catalog quality inferred by the evaluation of metadata and dataset characteristics
Portal quality evaluated through support and enablement mechanisms

Learn more about tracking data portal measures.


Engagement Measures
The toolkit also provides examples of public activity that confirm interest and use of open data including:

Attendance at events and outcomes
Questions for data owners
Support requests
Public information requests
Views of support content
Social media engagement
Registration to mail distribution lists
Intemediariy activity and contributions using open datasets or the creation of new datasets in:

Articles in local news websites and blogs
Analysis products
Tools
Advocacy
Enablement content, training, and events


Learn more about monitoring public engagement measures.


Reporting Practices
Finally, the toolkit shows how regular reporting enables organizations to link government and community priorities with actions and measures of progress.
Learn how to incorporate reporting practices and view examples of annual reports, blog posts, and analytic dashboards.
